introduction: These readings give one instruction many times over: in whatever country Bahá’ís live they are to be truthful, loyal and obedient to its government, to wish it well and pray for it, to serve honestly in any office they hold, and to keep out of faction and political agitation. Most were written to a small, mistrusted community in Persia under the Qajar shahs, and many praise a particular king or answer the charge of sedition. A hundred of the guide's hundred and thirty-three quotations are read here, ten from each tenth of the reading order, beside a hundred from elsewhere. Two thirds stand alongside: Paul and Peter on the powers that be, Jeremiah's letter to the exiles, Joseph and Daniel serving foreign kings, Proverbs on the throne, the Crito, and the old accusations of disloyalty made against Jews and early Christians. A third push back or add a side: the midwives who disobeyed Pharaoh, Antigone, Socrates and Peter obeying God rather than men, Locke, Thoreau, Douglass, the consent of the governed, and the voices from Confucius to Saadi who lay the heavier duty on the ruler.
questions: The readings ask for obedience, truthfulness and goodwill toward government. Which of the three is hardest, and why might all three be asked together?
Someone asks in the readings how an unjust government can be obeyed. Set the answer beside the Hebrew midwives, Antigone and Peter's 'obey God rather than men'. Where is the line?
Jews in Persia and Christians in Rome were both accused of disloyalty. How does a minority show its loyalty, and what can it not prove?
Confucius, Saadi and Deuteronomy put duties on the ruler. Do the readings assume a just ruler, or ask obedience regardless?
Pericles thought the citizen who stays out of public affairs useless; the readings forbid political talk. What can be done for a country without partisanship?
Many readings praise a shah by name. How would you read them now, under a different kind of government?

outside.why: Paul writes that every soul should be subject to the higher powers, for the powers that be are ordained of God.
Jeremiah wrote to the exiles in Babylon to seek the peace of the city where they had been carried, and to pray for it.
The letter to Titus asks believers to obey magistrates, be ready for every good work, and speak evil of no man.
Peter asks submission to king and governors for the Lord's sake, so that well doing may silence the ignorance of foolish men.
Pharaoh set Joseph, a foreigner of another faith, over his house, because none was so discreet and wise as he.
Daniel served a foreign king so faithfully that his rivals could find neither error nor fault in him.
John the Baptist told tax collectors to exact no more than was appointed, and soldiers to do violence to no man.
Jesus, shown the coin with Caesar's image, said to render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's.
Wisdom says in Proverbs: by me kings reign and princes decree justice, and all the judges of the earth.
Told by the council to stop teaching, Peter answered that we ought to obey God rather than men. Where would the readings place that line?
Peter's letter puts it in four short commands: honour all men, love the brotherhood, fear God, honour the king.
Paul asks that prayers be made for kings and all in authority, that people may lead a quiet and peaceable life.
Daniel blesses the God who changes the times and the seasons, who removes kings and sets up kings.
Jesus blessed the peacemakers, and said that they shall be called the children of God.
Proverbs counsels: fear the Lord and the king, and do not meddle with those who are given to change.
Paul adds that tribute should be paid, and each given his due: tribute, custom, fear and honour to whom they are owed.
David's last words say that he who rules over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God. Is obedience owed because of a ruler's justice, or apart from it?
Jesus told Pilate that his kingdom was not of this world; if it were, his servants would fight.
Confucius puts the weight on the ruler: one who governs by virtue is like the pole star, toward which all the stars turn. What does that ask of the governed?
The American Declaration holds that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. How does well-wishing obedience differ from consent?
Micah sums up what is required: to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.
Jesus told his disciples that whoever would be great among them must be their minister, and the chief their servant.
Proverbs says that a man diligent in his business shall stand before kings, and not before mean men.
When Samuel presented Saul to the tribes, all the people shouted and said, God save the king.
Confucius, asked what more should be done for a numerous people, answered: enrich them, and then teach them.
Confucius likens superiors and inferiors to wind and grass: the grass must bend when the wind blows across it.
Proverbs holds that righteousness exalts a nation, while sin is a reproach to any people.
Washington grants that parties, within limits, may be useful checks on government and keep alive the spirit of liberty. What is lost, and what is kept, by standing aside from them?
Ecclesiastes counsels keeping the king's commandment, for where the word of a king is, there is power.
Paul says rulers are a terror not to good works but to evil, and calls the ruler a minister of God for good.
Thoreau asks whether a citizen must ever resign his conscience to the legislator, and says we should be men first and subjects afterward. What do the readings answer?
Asked whether his master paid the tribute, Peter said yes; Jesus, though he questioned who owes it, had it paid.
In Plato's Crito the laws tell Socrates that he must do what his city and country order, or else change their view of what is just.
A saying of Muhammad makes everyone a guardian answerable for his charge, the ruler for his subjects. If the nation owes obedience, what does the ruler owe?
Burke held that a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation. How should a people's wishes reach those who govern?
Proverbs says that where no counsel is the people fall, but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
The Qur'an likewise tells believers to obey God, to obey the messenger, and those among them who are in authority.
Ecclesiastes advises: curse not the king, even in thy thought, for a bird of the air shall carry the voice.
A psalm prays for the ruler: give the king thy judgments, O God, that he may judge the poor and break the oppressor.
Mencius ranked the people as the most important element in a nation and the sovereign as the lightest. Does loyalty look different when seen from there?
The law given in Exodus says: thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people.
The book of Ezra opens with a Persian king, Cyrus, letting an exiled people go up and rebuild the house of their God.
Isaiah calls the Persian king Cyrus the Lord's anointed, whose right hand God has held.
Proverbs says that the king by judgment establishes the land, but he that receives gifts overthrows it.
Proverbs holds that mercy and truth preserve the king, and that his throne is upheld by mercy.
A psalm warns: put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. How far should praise of a ruler go?
Proverbs says it is an abomination for kings to commit wickedness, for the throne is established by righteousness.
Proverbs again: take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness.
Shakespeare's sleepless king envies his poorest subject's rest: uneasy lies the head that wears a crown. What might a prayer for a ruler ask for?
Acton wrote that power tends to corrupt and absolute power corrupts absolutely. Can gratitude to a ruler live beside that caution?
David, hunted by Saul and with the king in his power, would not put forth his hand against the Lord's anointed.
A king in Hamlet says that such divinity hedges a king that treason can only peep at what it would do.
Saadi tells kings that the sheep is not for the shepherd, but the shepherd for the service of the sheep. What does a just government owe its people?
The Hebrew midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them. When, if ever, is that the right course?
Antigone tells her king that his decrees cannot override the unwritten and unfailing statutes of heaven. Is there a line the readings would also draw?
Locke held that rulers who try to take away the people's property or enslave them put themselves in a state of war with the people. Where do the readings part from him?
A psalm says that some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will remember the name of the Lord our God.
Proverbs says a king's honour is in the multitude of his people, and the want of people is the destruction of the prince.
Shakespeare's King Richard says that all the water in the sea cannot wash the balm from an anointed king, nor men depose the Lord's deputy.
Daniel, unharmed among the lions, greets the king who put him there with 'O king, live for ever', and says he has done him no hurt.
Confucius named food, arms and the confidence of the people as what government requires. Whose work is it to earn that confidence?
Proverbs says the king's heart is in the hand of the Lord, who turns it like rivers of water wherever he will.
Socrates told his court that he honoured and loved the men of Athens, but would obey God rather than them. How does that sit with 'the greatest obligation'?
The Qur'an addresses God as the Owner of sovereignty, who gives it to whom he will and withdraws it from whom he will.
Paul tells the Galatians that they are called to liberty, and should use it by love to serve one another.
Paul speaks of providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord but also in the sight of men.
Isaiah says: in returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength.
Old counsellors told a new king: if thou wilt be a servant unto this people, they will be thy servants for ever. Does loyalty run in both directions?
Ecclesiastes says woe to the land whose king is a child, and blessed the land whose princes eat for strength. What does a new reign need from its subjects?
The second psalm speaks to rulers directly: be wise now, O ye kings; be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
Pericles said that Athens regards the man who takes no part in public duties not as unambitious but as useless. Why might a community choose silence on politics all the same?
Paul tells the Colossians: whatever you do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
Jesus was accused before Pilate of perverting the nation and forbidding tribute to Caesar: a charge of disloyalty laid on the surface of things.
Hebrews speaks of those who confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth and desired a better country.
Habakkuk is told that the vision is for an appointed time: though it tarry, wait for it.
Paul tells the Thessalonians to study to be quiet, to do their own business, and to work with their own hands.
The law in Exodus says: thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil, nor lean after many to wrest judgment.
Samuel told Saul that to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
Jethro advised Moses to choose able men who fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness, and set them as rulers.
Plato thought cities would have no rest until philosophers were kings, or kings took up philosophy. What would 'politics of the right type' look like?
The centurion tells Jesus that he is a man set under authority, with soldiers under him who go and come at his word.
Shakespeare's Henry V says that every subject's duty is the king's, but every subject's soul is his own. Where does the duty of office end?
Tennyson's cavalry rode on: theirs not to reason why, theirs but to do and die. Is unquestioning obedience a virtue only when the general is known to be the true one?
Haman told the Persian king of a scattered people whose laws were different and who did not keep the king's laws: the charge every minority fears.
Paul's accuser before the governor called him a pestilent fellow and a mover of sedition, ringleader of a sect.
Enemies wrote to the Persian king that the returned exiles were building a rebellious city and would pay no toll or tribute.
At Thessalonica the first Christians were accused of turning the world upside down and acting against the decrees of Caesar.
Pilate was told that if he let Jesus go he was not Caesar's friend: loyalty to the ruler used as a weapon by accusers.
The Universal Declaration says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government. Does the form of a government change the duty owed to it?
Three officials of Babylon told their king that they would not serve his gods, whatever followed. Is there an obedience the readings too would withhold?
In the Qur'an the lost say: we obeyed our princes and great men, and they misled us from the way. Does obedience remove a person's own responsibility?
Paul writes that what is required in stewards, before anything else, is that a man be found faithful.
Proverbs observes that when the righteous are in authority the people rejoice, but when the wicked bear rule the people mourn. Is happiness under government only in the subject's hands?
Deuteronomy binds the king as well: on his throne he must write out a copy of the law and read in it. What stands above a throne?
The master in the parable says: well done, good and faithful servant; thou hast been faithful over a few things.
Thoreau wrote that under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison. What would the readings say to him?
Confucius said that to govern means to rectify: lead with correctness, and who will dare not to be correct? Whose conduct has to come first?
Douglass said that without struggle there is no progress, and that those who deprecate agitation want crops without plowing. What other road to progress do the readings trust?
Shakespeare's Isabella sees proud man, dressed in a little brief authority, playing tricks that make the angels weep. How is a subject to regard such a ruler?
Paul's counsel to the Romans: if it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.

titus-subject-to-principalities.text: Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work, To speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle, shewing all meekness unto all men

peter-submit-to-every-ordinance.text: Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme; Or unto governors, as unto them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well. For so is the will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men

ecclesiastes-curse-not-the-king.text: Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter

proverbs-fear-the-lord-and-the-king.text: My son, fear thou the Lord and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change

proverbs-by-me-kings-reign.text: By me kings reign, and princes decree justice. By me princes rule, and nobles, even all the judges of the earth

romans-tribute-to-whom-tribute.text: For for this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God's ministers, attending continually upon this very thing. Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour

ecclesiastes-keep-the-kings-commandment.text: I counsel thee to keep the king's commandment, and that in regard of the oath of God. Be not hasty to go out of his sight: stand not in an evil thing; for he doeth whatsoever pleaseth him. Where the word of a king is, there is power: and who may say unto him, What doest thou

exodus-nor-curse-the-ruler.text: Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people

daniel-most-high-ruleth.text: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men

matthew-tribute-money-fish.text: And when they were come to Capernaum, they that received tribute money came to Peter, and said, Doth not your master pay tribute? He saith, Yes. And when he was come into the house, Jesus prevented him, saying, What thinkest thou, Simon? of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? of their own children, or of strangers? Peter saith unto him, Of strangers. Jesus saith unto him, Then are the children free. Notwithstanding, lest we should offend them, go thou to the sea, and cast an hook, and take up the fish that first cometh up; and when thou hast opened his mouth, thou shalt find a piece of money: that take, and give unto them for me and thee

samuel-god-save-the-king.text: And Samuel said to all the people, See ye him whom the Lord hath chosen, that there is none like him among all the people? And all the people shouted, and said, God save the king

genesis-joseph-over-my-house.text: And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, Forasmuch as God hath shewed thee all this, there is none so discreet and wise as thou art: Thou shalt be over my house, and according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled: only in the throne will I be greater than thou

exodus-midwives-feared-god.text: But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive

proverbs-mercy-and-truth-preserve-the-ki.text: Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy

proverbs-ruler-hearken-to-lies.text: If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked

luke-forbidding-tribute-to-caesar.text: And the whole multitude of them arose, and led him unto Pilate. And they began to accuse him, saying, We found this fellow perverting the nation, and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar, saying that he himself is Christ a King

esther-laws-diverse-from-all-people.text: And Haman said unto king Ahasuerus, There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the people in all the provinces of thy kingdom; and their laws are diverse from all people; neither keep they the king's laws: therefore it is not for the king's profit to suffer them

john-not-caesars-friend.text: And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him: but the Jews cried out, saying, If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar's friend: whosoever maketh himself a king speaketh against Caesar

acts-mover-of-sedition.text: For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes

ezra-rebellious-and-bad-city.text: Be it known unto the king, that the Jews which came up from thee to us are come unto Jerusalem, building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up the walls thereof, and joined the foundations. Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings

luke-man-set-under-authority.text: Lord, trouble not thyself: for I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof: Wherefore neither thought I myself worthy to come unto thee: but say in a word, and my servant shall be healed. For I also am a man set under authority, having under me soldiers, and I say unto one, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth it

proverbs-wicked-from-before-the-king.text: Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness

shakespeare-balm-from-an-anointed-king.text: Not all the water in the rough rude sea / Can wash the balm off from an anointed king; / The breath of worldly men cannot depose / The deputy elected by the Lord
shakespeare-balm-from-an-anointed-king.author: William Shakespeare

plato-do-what-his-country-orders.text: whether in battle or in a court of law, or in any other place, he must do what his city and his country order him; or he must change their view of what is just
plato-do-what-his-country-orders.author: Plato

tennyson-theirs-not-to-reason-why.text: Their's not to reason why, / Their's not to make reply, / Their's but to do and die
tennyson-theirs-not-to-reason-why.author: Alfred Tennyson
tennyson-theirs-not-to-reason-why.work: The Charge of the Light Brigade

thoreau-men-first-subjects-afterward.text: Must the citizen ever for a moment, or in the least degree, resign his conscience to the legislator? Why has every man a conscience, then? I think that we should be men first, and subjects afterward
thoreau-men-first-subjects-afterward.author: Henry David Thoreau
